question: Figure (i) shows an imaginary cube of edge length $L$. A uniformly charged rod of length $2L$ moves towards left at a small but constant speed $v$. At $t = 0$, the left end of the rod just touches the centre of the face of the cube opposite to it. Which of the graphs shown in fig. (ii) represents the flux of the electric field through the cube as the rod goes through it?
solution:
According to Gauss's Law, the total electric flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{E}}$ passing through any closed Gaussian surface depends only on the net electric charge enclosed inside the surface.

$$ \Phi_{\mathrm{E}}=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}}{\varepsilon_0} $$

Let $\mathrm{L}=$ edge length of the cube, $2 \mathrm{~L}=$ total length of the uniformly charged rod, $\lambda=$ uniform linear charge density of the rod (constant throughout its length)

If $\mathrm{v}=$ constant speed of the rod moving to the left then $\mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t})=$ length of the rod currently enclosed within the cube at time t.

The charge enclosed inside the cube at any time t is directly proportional to the enclosed length.

$$ \mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}(\mathrm{t})=\lambda \cdot \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) $$

Therefore, the flux at time t is $\Phi_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{t})=\frac{\lambda \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t})}{\varepsilon_0}$

Since $\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon_0}$ is constant, the graph of flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{t})$ versus time t must be in the shape of the enclosed length x(t) versus time t.

Let the entry face be at position $\mathrm{x}=0$ and the opposite exit face be at distance $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{L}$ inside the cube.

At $\mathrm{t}=0$, the left end just enters the cube, so the enclosed length is $\mathrm{x}(0)=0$.

As time increases, the front end of the rod travels across the cube until it reaches the opposite face at distance L.

During this period, the enclosed length is $\mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{vt}$

Thus, the flux increases linearly with time $\Phi_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{t})=\left(\frac{\lambda \mathrm{v}}{\varepsilon_0}\right) \mathrm{t}$

The time taken by left end to reach the left face of cube is equal to time taken to cover the distance L with speed $\mathrm{v}, \Delta \mathrm{t}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{v}}$.

At $\mathrm{t}_1=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{v}}$, the entire cube width is occupied by the rod $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{L} \Rightarrow \Phi_{\text {max }}=\frac{\lambda \mathrm{L}}{\varepsilon_0}$

Hence, the rod is entering the cube from $\mathrm{t}=0$ to $\mathrm{t}_1=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{v}}$ and magnetic flux is changing linearly with time.

Since the total length of the rod is 2 L , when the front end exits the left face, there is still an additional length of L remaining outside behind the right face.

Therefore, the length of the rod inside the cube remains constant at $\mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{L}$.

The flux remains constant at its maximum value $\Phi_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{t})=\frac{\lambda \mathrm{L}}{\varepsilon_0}=$ constant

The duration of this constant phase is $\Delta \mathrm{t}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~L}-\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{v}}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{v}}$

Hence, when the rod is passing through the cube at full capacity from $\mathrm{t}_1=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{v}}$ to $\mathrm{t}_2=\frac{2 \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{v}}$, the electric flux is constant.

At $\mathrm{t}_2=\frac{2 \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{v}}$, the rear end of the rod enters the right face of the cube.

The length remaining inside the cube decreases linearly

$$ \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t})=2 \mathrm{~L}-\mathrm{v}\left(\mathrm{t}-\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{v}}\right)=3 \mathrm{~L}-\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{t}} $$

Thus, the flux decreases linearly with time back to zero. $\Phi_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{t})=\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon_0}(3 \mathrm{~L}-\mathrm{vt})$

At $\mathrm{t}_3=\frac{3 \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{v}}$, the rear end fully leaves the cube, and the flux becomes zero.

Hence, when the rod is exiting the cube from $\mathrm{t}_2=\frac{2 \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{v}}$ to $\mathrm{t}_3=\frac{3 \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{v}}$, the electric flux is decreasing at constant rate (linearly).

Therefore, the resulting graph starts at zero, rises with a constant positive slope, maintains a horizontal flat maximum, and then decreases with a constant negative slope back to zero.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

question: Eight point charges (can be assumed as uniformly charged small spheres and their centres at the corner of the cube) having value $q$ each are fixed at vertices of a cube. The electric flux through square surface ABCD of the cube is
solution:
Considering a single point charge q placed precisely at one vertex of a cube.

At any corner of a cube, space can be divided symmetrically into 8 identical adjacent cubes meeting at that single common corner.

By Gauss's Law, the total electric flux outward from an isolated point charge q into all space enclosing the charge is $\Phi_{\text {total }}=\mathrm{q} / \varepsilon_0$

Because the 8 identical cubes meeting at that vertex are symmetric and together surround the charge over all, therefore, the total flux entering inside any one of the 8 cubes from that single corner charge is.

$$ \Phi_{\text {cube }, 1 \text { corner }}=\frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\varepsilon_0}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{8 \varepsilon_0} $$

A cube has 6 square faces. For a charge located at a given corner:

3 adjacent faces meet directly at that corner.

For these 3 faces, the electric field lines radiate outwards radially from the vertex along the planes of the faces themselves. Hence, the electric field vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ is parallel to the surface of each adjacent face, i.e., $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \perp \mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}$.

So, the electric flux through these faces is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=0$, so the electric flux through each of the 3 adjacent faces is zero.

$$ \Phi_{\text {adjacent }}=0 $$

The remaining flux $\frac{\mathrm{q}}{8 \varepsilon_0}$ must exit the cube through 3 opposite faces. Since the geometry of these 3 opposite faces is identical relative to the given corner, the flux divides equally among them by symmetry.

$$ \Phi_{\text {opposite face, } 1 \text { corner }}=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{\mathrm{q}}{8 \varepsilon_0}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{24 \varepsilon_0} $$

The cube has 8 identical point charges of value q at all 8 of its vertices

The vertices A, B, C, and D lie on the boundary of the square face ABCD.

For each of these 4 charges, the face ABCD is an adjacent face., so the electric field lines originating from a vertex lie in the plane of its adjacent faces $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \perp \mathrm{da})$.

Therefore, the flux contributed to the face ABCD by the 4 charges on $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}$, and D is

$$ \Phi_{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{~B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}}=0+0+0+0=0 $$

The remaining 4 vertices lie on the opposite face parallel to ABCD. For each of these 4 distant charges, the face ABCD is one of their 3 symmetric opposite faces.

Therefore, each of these 4 charges independently contributes an equal flux to face ABCD

$$ \Phi_{\text {each }}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{24 \varepsilon_0} $$

Hence, total electric flux through face ABCD is the sum of electric flux from all 8 charges by the principle of superposition.

$$ \Phi_{\mathrm{ABCD}}=4 \times\left(\frac{\mathrm{q}}{24 \varepsilon_0}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{6 \varepsilon_0} $$

Thus, the correct option is (C).

question: Figure shows two large cylindrical shells having uniform linear charge densities $+\lambda$ and $-\lambda$. Radius of inner cylinder is 'a' and that of outer cylinder is 'b'. A charged particle of mass $m$, charge $q$ revolves in a circle of radius $r$. Then, its speed 'v' is: (Neglect gravity and assume the radii of both the cylinders to be very small in comparison to their length.)
solution:
The two cylindrical shells of infinite length are coaxial.

Inner cylinder has radius a and linear charge density $+\lambda$.

Outer cylinder has radius b and linear charge density $-\lambda$.

The charged particle orbits in a circle of radius r , where $\mathrm{a}<\mathrm{r}<\mathrm{b}$.

By Gauss's law, due to cylindrical symmetry, the electric field is purely radial $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{E}(\mathrm{r}) \hat{\mathrm{r}})$ and proportional to the charge enclosed in the Gaussian surface.

For a Gaussian surface of radius $a

$$\Phi_E = \frac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E(r)(2\pi r l) = \frac{\lambda \times l}{\varepsilon_0}$$

$$\Rightarrow E(r) = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 r}$$

The particle has mass $m$, charge $q$, and orbits at radius $r$ with speed $v$.

For stable circular motion under the electrostatic force, the radial electrostatic force must provide the necessary centripetal force directed toward the axis of rotation.

$$F_e = F_c$$

If charge is $q$ and kept in electric field $E(r)$ then electrostatic force is

$$F_e = qE(r) = q\left(\frac{\lambda}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 r}\right) = \frac{\lambda q}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 r}$$

The centripetal force required to sustain a circular path of radius $r$ at speed $v$ is

$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{\lambda q}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 r}$$

$$v^2 = \frac{\lambda q}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 m} \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda q}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 m}}$$

Thus, the correct option is (A).

$$ \oint_{\mathrm{S}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}}{\varepsilon_0} $$

The electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ is the net electric field at any point on the Gaussian surface.

The electric flux represents the electric field lines linking to the given closed surface.

According to the principle of superposition, the net electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ at any position $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}$ in space is the vector sum of the electric fields produced by every single charge present in the universe, regardless of whether each charge is situated inside or outside the Gaussian surface.

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}})=\sum\limits_{\mathrm{i}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{i}}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}})=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{rq}_1}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{-\mathrm{q}_1}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{q}_2} $$

Here, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{+\mathrm{q}_1}$ is the field due to $+\mathrm{q}_1, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{-\mathrm{q}_1}$ is the field due to $-\mathrm{q}_1$ and the field due to $\mathrm{q}_2$ is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{q}_2}$.

Thus, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{+\mathrm{q}_1}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{-\mathrm{q}_1}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{q}_2}$

The flux through the given closed surface due to charge outside the surface is zero because number of electric field lines entering the surface is equal to exiting the surface, i.e., $\oint_{\mathrm{S}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{q}_2} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=0$

However, at any point on the surface $S$, the electric field $\vec{E}_{q_2}$ produced by $q_2$ is generally non-zero.

Therefore, the total electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ at points on the spherical Gaussian surface is the resultant field produced by all the charges $\left(+\mathrm{q}_1,-\mathrm{q}_1\right.$, and \left.\mathrm{q}_2\right).

question: 1 μC charge is uniformly distributed on a spherical shell given by equation $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 25$. What will be intensity of electric field at a point $(1, 1, 2)$?
solution:
The general equation of of a sphere centredat the origin $(0,0,0)$ is $x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2$ where $R$ is the radius of sphere.

The given equation of the spherical shell is $\mathrm{x}^2+\mathrm{y}^2+\mathrm{z}^2=25$

Therefore, the radius R of the shell is $\mathrm{R}=\sqrt{25}=5$ units

The point where the electric field is to be calculated is P(1, 1, 2).

The radial distance r from the origin to point P is

$$ r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{1^2+1^2+2^2}=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt{6} \text { units } $$

Since $\sqrt{6} \approx 2.45, \mathrm{r}<\mathrm{R}(\sqrt{6}<5)$, point P lies inside the uniformly charged spherical shell.

For a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius r centredat (0, 0, 0), where r < R.

question: The net electric field on two sides of an infinite sheet is shown in the figure. Assume that the sheet is placed in a uniform electric field. The surface charge density of the sheet is given by $\mathbf{n} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{0}}$. The value of n is.
solution:
Let the infinite planar thin sheet carrying a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$ (assuming $\sigma>0$ ).

The electric field is perpendicular pointing outward from the positively charged sheet.

By Gauss's law, $\mathrm{E}_{\text {sheet }}=\frac{\sigma}{2 \epsilon_0}$

Thus, the infinite charged sheet produces a uniform electric field of magnitude $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ pointing away from it on both sides.

Let the sheet lie in the $yz$-plane, and let an external uniform electric field $\vec{E}_{\mathrm{ext}} = E_0\hat{\imath}$ be applied across the region.

To the right side of the sheet $(+x$ direction$)$ the field due to the sheet points in the $+\hat{\imath}$ direction

$$\vec{E}_{\mathrm{right}} = \left(E_0 + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\right)\hat{\imath}$$

Given the net field on this side has magnitude $E_2 = 12\,\mathrm{V/m}$ directed to the right.

$$E_0 + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = 12 \ldots (\mathrm{i})$$

To the left side of the sheet $(-x$ direction$)$, the field due to the sheet points in the $-\hat{\imath}$ direction.

$$\vec{E}_{\mathrm{left}} = \left(E_0 - \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\right)\hat{\imath}$$

The net electric field on the left side is $E_1 = 8\ \mathrm{V/m}$ directed to the right (in the same direction, $+\hat{\imath}$).

$$E_0 - \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = 8 \ldots (\mathrm{ii})$$

Subtracting equation $(\mathrm{ii})$ from equation $(\mathrm{i})$,

$$\left(E_0 + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\right) - \left(E_0 - \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\right) = 12 - 8$$

$$\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = 4$$

$$\sigma = 4\varepsilon_0 = n\varepsilon_0 \Rightarrow n = 4$$

Therefore, the value of $n$ is 4.

question: A uniform electric field $\mathrm{E}=500 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{C}$ passes through a hemispherical surface of radius $\mathrm{R}=1.2 \mathrm{~m}$ as shown in figure. If the net electric flux (in SI units) through the hemispherical surface only is $N \pi$, then find the value of $N$.
solution:
The given surface is an open hemispherical of radius $R = 1.2\text{ m}$.

To apply Gauss's law, the surface should be closed. To close this hemisphere, we can add a flat circular base of radius $R$ at the bottom.

Together, the curved hemispherical surface and the flat circular base form a complete closed surface containing zero enclosed charge ($q_{\text{enclosed}} = 0$).

question: A sphere of radius $R$ has charge density given by $\rho=\rho_0\left(1-\frac{n r}{3 R}\right)$, where $\rho_0$ is a constant, $r$ is distance from centre of sphere. For a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $R$ centred at the centre of sphere, the flux is zero. Find $n$.
solution:
According to Gauss's law the total electric flux $\Phi$ through any closed surface is proportional to the net charge enclosed within that surface.

$$ \Phi=\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}}=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}}{\epsilon_0} $$

It is given that the electric flux through the spherical Gaussian surface of radius R is zero:

$$ \Phi=0 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}}{\epsilon_0}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}=0 $$

The charge density $\rho(\mathrm{r})$ depends only on the radial distance r from the centre.

For a thin concentric spherical shell of radius $r$ and thickness $dr$, the volume of this thin spherical shell is

$$dV = 4\text{π } r^2 \, dr$$

The infinitesimal charge $dq$ contained within this shell is

$$dq = \rho(r)dV = \rho_0 \left(1 - \frac{nr}{3R}\right) \left(4\text{π } r^2 \, dr\right)$$

The total charge enclosed within the entire sphere of radius $R$ is obtained by integrating $dq$ from $r = 0$ to $r = R$.

$$q_{\text{enclosed}} = \int\limits_{0}^{R} dq = \int\limits_{0}^{R} 4\text{π } \rho_0 \left(1 - \frac{nr}{3R}\right) r^2 \, dr$$

$$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 4\text{π } \rho_0 \int\limits_{0}^{R} \left(r^2 - \frac{n r^3}{3R}\right) dr$$

$$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 4\text{π } \rho_0 \left[ \left.\frac{r^3}{3}\right|_{0}^{R} - \frac{n}{3R} \left.\frac{r^4}{4}\right|_{0}^{R} \right] = 4\text{π } \rho_0 \left[ \frac{R^3}{3} - \frac{n}{3R} \left(\frac{R^4}{4}\right) \right]$$

$$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 4\text{π } \rho_0 \left[ \frac{R^3}{3} - \frac{nR^3}{12} \right]$$

$$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 4\text{π } \rho_0 R^3 \left(\frac{4-n}{12}\right) = \frac{\pi \, \rho_0 \, R^3 (4-n)}{3}$$

Since $\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{\pi \rho_0 \mathrm{R}^3(4-\mathrm{n})}{3}=0$. Since $\pi, \rho_0$, and R are non-zero constants.

$$ \Rightarrow 4-\mathrm{n}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=4 $$

Therefore, the value of n is 4 .

question: The length of each side of a cubical closed surface is $l$. A charge $q$ is situated on one of the vertices of the cube as shown in figure. The flux passing through shaded faces of the cube is $\frac{q}{n \epsilon_0}$. Find $n$.
solution:
A corner vertex in three-dimensional space is where 8 identical cubes can meet at a single point to enclose a charge symmetrically.

By Gauss's law, the total electric flux emerging symmetrically in all directions from a point charge q is $\Phi_{\text {total }}=$ $\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\epsilon_0}$.

Since the corner vertex is shared equally among 8 identical cubes, the fraction of the total flux entering the single given cube is $\Phi_{\text {cube }}=\frac{\Phi_{\text {total }}}{8}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{8 \epsilon_0}$

A cube has 6 planar faces.

3 of the faces meet at the vertex where the charge q is located.

For each of these three faces, any electric field line originating from the charge q lies within the plane of the face, i.e., the electric field vector $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the area vector $d\vec{a}$, so $\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{a} = 0$.

Therefore, the electric flux through each of the 3 adjacent faces is zero $\Phi_{\text{adjacent faces}} = 0$

By the cubic symmetry with respect to the charge at the corner, each of the remaining 3 opposite faces subtends the same solid angle with respect to the charge.

Therefore, the entire flux that enters the cube $\left(\dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}\right)$ passes equally through these 3 opposite faces.

$$\Phi_{\text{each opposite face}} = \dfrac{\Phi_{\text{cube}}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}\right) = \dfrac{q}{24\varepsilon_0}$$

Out of the shaded faces, the top face does not contain the bottom vertex $(\Phi_{\text{each opposite face}})$, the bottom face contains the vertex $(\Phi_{\text{adjacent faces}})$ and the right face also does not contain the vertex $(\Phi_{\text{each opposite face}})$.

Therefore, the total flux passing through the shaded faces is

$$\Phi_{\text{shaded}} = \Phi_{\text{top}} + \Phi_{\text{right}} + \Phi_{\text{bottom}} = \dfrac{q}{24\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{q}{24\varepsilon_0} + 0 = \dfrac{2q}{24\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{q}{12\varepsilon_0}$$

$$\Rightarrow \Phi_{\text{shaded}} = \dfrac{q}{n\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{q}{12\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow n = 12$$

Therefore, the value of n is 12.

question: A point charge $+q$ is placed on the axis of a closed cylinder of radius $R$ and height $\frac{25 R}{12}$ as shown. If electric flux coming out from the curved surface of cylinder is $\frac{x q}{10 \epsilon_0}$, then calculate $x$.
solution:
Let a point charge q be placed at the origin. Consider a circular disk of radius R located at a perpendicular distance d from the charge along its central axis.

The electric field produced by the point charge at a distance r is $\mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{r}^2}$

To find the flux through the disk, let a thin ring of radius y and width dy on the disk.

Distance from the charge to this ring $\mathrm{r}=\sqrt{\mathrm{d}^2+\mathrm{y}^2}$

The area of this elemental ring is $\mathrm{dA}=2 \pi \mathrm{y} \mathrm{dy}$

The normal vector to the disk is along the axis. The angle $\theta$ between the electric field and the normal to the disk is, $\cos \theta=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{d}^2+\mathrm{y}^2}}$

The electric flux through this differential ring is $d \Phi=E \cos \theta d A=\left(\frac{q}{4 \pi \epsilon_0\left(d^2+y^2\right)}\right)\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{d^2+y^2}}\right)(2 \pi y d y)$

$$ \mathrm{d} \Phi=\frac{\mathrm{qd}}{2 \epsilon_0} \frac{\mathrm{ydy}}{\left(\mathrm{~d}^2+\mathrm{y}^2\right)^{3 / 2}} $$

Total flux is the sum from 0 to R is, $\Phi_{\text {disk }}=\frac{\mathrm{qd}}{2 \epsilon_0} \int\limits_0^{\mathrm{R}} \frac{\mathrm{y}}{\left(\mathrm{d}^2+\mathrm{y}^2\right)^{3 / 2}} \mathrm{dy}$

Let $\mathrm{u}=\mathrm{d}^2+\mathrm{y}^2$, so $\mathrm{du}=2 \mathrm{y} \mathrm{dy}$,

$$ \Phi_{\mathrm{disk}}=\frac{\mathrm{qd}}{2 \epsilon_0}\left[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{~d}^2+\mathrm{y}^2}}\right]_0^{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{\mathrm{q} 2}{\epsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{~d}^2}+\mathrm{R}^2}\right) $$

The semi-vertical angle $\alpha$ subtended by the rim of the disk at the charge $\left(\cos \alpha=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{d}^2+\mathrm{R}^2}}\right)$.

$$ \Phi_{\mathrm{disk}}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{2 \epsilon_0}(1-\cos \alpha) $$

The point charge +q is completely enclosed inside the closed cylinder. By Gauss's law, the total flux emerging out of the entire closed cylinder is $\Phi_{\text {total }}=\mathrm{q} / \epsilon_0$

The total surface of the cylinder consists of three parts, the left circular base (disk 1), the right circular base (disk 2) and the curved surface.

The distance of the charge $+q$ from the left circular face is $d_1 = \frac{4R}{3}$. The radius of the face is $R$.

$$\frac{d_1}{\sqrt{d_1^2 + R^2}} = \frac{4R/3}{5R/3} = \frac{4}{5}$$

Using the derived disk formula for flux,

$$\Phi_{\text{left disk}} = \frac{q}{2\epsilon_0} \left(1 - \frac{4}{5}\right) = \frac{q}{2\epsilon_0} \left(\frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{q}{10\epsilon_0}$$

The distance of the charge $+q$ from the right circular face is $d_2 = \frac{3R}{4}$ and the radius of the face is $R$.

$$\sqrt{d_2^2 + R^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{3R}{4}\right)^2 + R^2} = \sqrt{\frac{9R^2}{16} + R^2} = \sqrt{\frac{25R^2}{16}} = \frac{5R}{4}$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}_2}{\sqrt{\mathrm{d}_2^2 + R^2}} = \frac{3R/4}{5R/4} = \frac{3}{5}$$

Using the derived disk formula for flux,

$$\Phi_{\text{right disk}} = \frac{q}{2\epsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{3}{5}\right) = \frac{q}{2\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) = \frac{2q}{10\epsilon_0} = \frac{q}{5\epsilon_0}$$

So, electric flux through the curved surface is

$$\Phi_{\text{curved}} = \frac{q}{\epsilon_0} - \left(\frac{q}{10\epsilon_0} + \frac{2q}{10\epsilon_0}\right)$$

$$\Phi_{\text{curved}} = \frac{q}{\epsilon_0} - \frac{3q}{10\epsilon_0} = \frac{7q}{10\epsilon_0} = \frac{xq}{10\epsilon_0} \Rightarrow x = 7$$

Therefore, the value of x is 7.
